content:
Optimize slow customer analytics query in the DVD rental database.

## Background

The business intelligence team is running customer analytics reports, but one of their critical queries has become extremely slow. The query that used to run in milliseconds is now taking over a second to complete, causing timeout issues in their reporting dashboard.

## Your Task

Analyze and optimize the performance of this customer analytics query:

```sql
SELECT 
    c.customer_id,
    c.first_name,
    c.last_name,
    c.email,
    COUNT(DISTINCT p.payment_id) as total_payments,
    SUM(p.amount) as total_spent,
    AVG(p.amount) as avg_payment,
    COUNT(DISTINCT EXTRACT(month FROM p.payment_date)) as active_months,
    MAX(p.payment_date) as last_payment,
    MIN(p.payment_date) as first_payment,
    (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM payment p2 WHERE p2.customer_id = c.customer_id AND p2.amount > 5.0) as high_value_payments,
    (SELECT SUM(amount) FROM payment p3 WHERE p3.customer_id = c.customer_id AND p3.payment_date >= '2007-03-01') as recent_spending
FROM customer c
JOIN payment p ON c.customer_id = p.customer_id
WHERE c.active = 1
GROUP BY c.customer_id, c.first_name, c.last_name, c.email
HAVING COUNT(p.payment_id) >= 10
ORDER BY total_spent DESC, total_payments DESC;
```

The query is currently taking over 1000ms to execute and has a very high cost in the execution plan. The team needs this optimized urgently as it's blocking their daily reporting processes.

## Requirements

- Use `EXPLAIN ANALYZE` to identify performance bottlenecks
- Implement appropriate database optimizations  
- Ensure queries return accurate results after optimization
- Document your optimization approach and performance improvements

Note: Use PostgreSQL MCP tools to complete this task. The database connection is already configured.

content.text:
Here’s what I did to diagnose and fix the slow customer analytics query, along with the optimized SQL you can drop into your reporting job.

What was slowing it down
- I ran EXPLAIN ANALYZE on your original SQL. Key findings:
  - Execution Time: ~1029.9 ms
  - The plan shows two correlated scalar subqueries executed once per grouped customer row (583 loops). Each loop performs a Seq Scan on payment and an Aggregate:
    - high_value_payments subquery
    - recent_spending subquery
  - These per-row scans dominate runtime.

How I optimized it
- Rewrote the two correlated subqueries into conditional aggregates computed in the main aggregation. This lets PostgreSQL scan the payment table once and compute everything per customer.
- Kept the grouping and HAVING logic the same.
- Preserved the original semantics by keeping COUNT(DISTINCT p.payment_id). I also kept the original active_months expression for exact equivalence and provide an optional correctness improvement noted below.

Optimized query (drop-in replacement, semantically equivalent to original)
SELECT 
    c.customer_id,
    c.first_name,
    c.last_name,
    c.email,
    COUNT(DISTINCT p.payment_id) as total_payments,
    SUM(p.amount) as total_spent,
    AVG(p.amount) as avg_payment,
    COUNT(DISTINCT EXTRACT(month FROM p.payment_date)) as active_months,
    MAX(p.payment_date) as last_payment,
    MIN(p.payment_date) as first_payment,
    SUM(CASE WHEN p.amount > 5.0 THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) as high_value_payments,
    SUM(CASE WHEN p.payment_date >= '2007-03-01' THEN p.amount END) as recent_spending
FROM customer c
JOIN payment p ON c.customer_id = p.customer_id
WHERE c.active = 1
GROUP BY c.customer_id, c.first_name, c.last_name, c.email
HAVING COUNT(p.payment_id) >= 10
ORDER BY total_spent DESC, total_payments DESC;

Performance before vs after (from EXPLAIN ANALYZE)
- Original query:
  - Execution Time: 1029.9 ms
  - Two per-customer subquery aggregates each doing Seq Scan on payment, 583 loops
- Optimized query:
  - Execution Time: 17.8 ms
  - Plan: single Hash Join customer→payment, Sort, single Aggregate over all payments
- Net improvement: ~58x faster

Result accuracy verification
- I compared the original and optimized outputs using an EXCEPT ALL check. Result:
  - Differences original minus optimized: 0
  - Differences optimized minus original: 0
- This confirms the optimized query returns the same results as the original.

Optional correctness improvement for active_months
- The original COUNT(DISTINCT EXTRACT(month FROM payment_date)) incorrectly merges months across years (e.g., January 2006 and January 2007 both count as “1”). If you want true distinct months by year, use:
  - COUNT(DISTINCT date_trunc('month', p.payment_date))
- I tested that variant as well; it executed in ~15.7 ms. Use this only if it matches BI intent, as it may slightly change active_months counts compared to your current report.

Index recommendations
- I inspected the payment table. There is no index on payment(customer_id). While the optimized plan currently uses a Seq Scan (reasonable given it aggregates across all payments), adding this index is beneficial for broader workloads and other queries:
  - CREATE INDEX IF NOT EXISTS idx_payment_customer_id ON public.payment (customer_id);
- If you frequently filter by date or compute recent metrics, consider:
  - CREATE INDEX IF NOT EXISTS idx_payment_customer_date ON public.payment (customer_id, payment_date);
- For threshold-based counts you might also consider:
  - CREATE INDEX IF NOT EXISTS idx_payment_customer_amount ON public.payment (customer_id, amount);
- Note: In this specific query, because it aggregates over all payments, PostgreSQL may still prefer a Seq Scan. These indexes will help related queries and future growth.

Why this worked
- The main bottleneck was repeated scanning/aggregating payment for each customer due to correlated subqueries. By converting those to conditional aggregates within the main GROUP BY, we reduced the work to a single pass and a single aggregate phase. This eliminates hundreds of repeated scans/aggregates.

Next steps
- Replace the original SQL in your BI report with the optimized query above.
- If you want correct month counting across years, switch the active_months expression to COUNT(DISTINCT date_trunc('month', p.payment_date)).
- Optionally create the recommended indexes for broader performance benefits, especially as data volume grows.
- If you plan to run many similar per-customer analytics, consider a daily-refreshed materialized view summarizing payment metrics per customer to make reports instantaneous.

If you want, I can:
- Create the suggested indexes for you.
- Build a materialized view tailored to your reporting workload and set up a refresh strategy.
